note: An experiment (GAME_SPEC §13.7, Stage 50; docs/CURRICULUM.md, experiment 6) on data/benches/hydrate.json: the formula of a hydrate. Blue copper sulfate crystals are weighed into a tared dish, heated until white, cooled and weighed again: the mass lost is their water. x = (water / 18.02) / (salt / 159.6), about 5.
title: Experiment: the water in blue crystals

steps.title: The dish on the balance
steps.text: Click the dish (the empty beaker) to pick it up, then click the balance to set it on its pan.
steps.why: This lab is read by instruments: nothing tells you what a vessel holds except what you measure. The analytical balance reads to a tenth of a milligram.

steps.title: Tare
steps.text: Right-click the balance to choose it, then click "tare" in the readout: it reads 0 with the empty dish on it.
steps.why: Taring takes the dish's own mass off the reading: from now on the balance reads only what you put in the dish. A balance reads a conventional mass, less the air a thing displaces; the dish displaces the same air before and after, so that cancels too.

steps.title: About 2 g of the crystals
steps.text: Pick up the jar, then right-click the dish for the menu. Type 2, then click "tip 2 g of the solid". Read what the balance says you took, and write it down.
steps.why: A hand never takes exactly what it aims at: you asked for about 2 g, and the balance tells you how much it was. That number, not the 2, is your sample's mass.

steps.title: Off the balance
steps.text: Pick up the dish and click a free square of the bench to set it down. The balance stays where it is.
steps.why: A balance is never heated: the dish goes to the burner, and back to the balance once it is cold.

steps.title: A burner under it
steps.text: Pick up the burner in the cabinet, then click the dish.

steps.title: Full flame
steps.text: Right-click the burner to choose it, then drag its valve fully open. Then click 60x on the clock to hurry the wait.
steps.why: Heated, the crystals give up their water in steps: CuSO4.5H2O to the trihydrate near 90 C, to the monohydrate near 110 C, and the last water only above about 200 C.

steps.title: Until it is white
steps.text: Watch the dish: the blue crystals pale to grey-white as their water leaves as steam.
steps.why: Anhydrous copper sulfate, CuSO4, is white. The blue was the water bound to the copper ions in the crystal.

checks.text: white copper sulfate in the dish

steps.title: Flame off, burner away
steps.text: Right-click the burner, drag its valve shut, then pick the burner up and put it back in the cabinet.

steps.title: Cold again
steps.text: Wait until the dish's thermometer reads the room's 20 C.
steps.why: A warm dish weighs light: its air is thinner than the room's, and on a tenth of a milligram that shows. Weigh only what is at the room's temperature.

steps.title: Back on the balance
steps.text: Pick up the dish and click the balance. It still has the empty dish's tare: it reads the white salt alone. Write it down.
steps.why: The crystals' mass less the salt's is the water. In moles: water / 18.02 g/mol and salt / 159.6 g/mol; their ratio is x in CuSO4.xH2O, which is 5. In a real lab the air is humid, and dry copper sulfate takes water back from it as it cools, so the result comes out a little under 5 unless the dish cools in a desiccator, a closed jar kept dry. This lab's air is dry.
